newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac inaugurates Algerian War monument.
newsitem.headline: Chirac inaugurates Algerian War monument.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac on Monday inaugurated a monument to the two million French soldiers, including himself, who fought unsuccessfully from 1952 to 1962 to keep Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia under France's flag.

"They dreamed of a more fraternal society (in the former North African possessions) which would have stayed forever tied to France," said Chirac, a junior officer in Algeria during his compulsory military service from 1956-1957.

Several thousand veterans of the North African campaigns, including a large contingent of Algerian Moslem auxiliaries who had to flee their native land for fear of repraisals at independence, attended the ceremony on a north Paris boulevard.
Chirac, who made no direct reference to his own experience, said his tribute was to those "who contributed to the grandeur of our country and France's civilising mission".

Morocco and Tunisia, then protectorates, were rapidly granted independence but Algeria, administratively part of France itself and with a large European minority, was the scene of a brutal struggle from 1954 to 1962.
The war quickly became unpopular in France and repeated atrocities were committed on both sides.

Although the French army held the upper hand thoughout the war, the then president Charles de Gaulle, believing the war isolated France diplomatically and held it back economically, directed a process which led to independence in July, 1962.
France lost 25,000 dead and says Algerian nationalist rebels lost up to 200,000 killed. Some Algerian historians have put the latter at 10 times that number.
